title: The Boarding House to the Speech Laboratory: Function Space, Feedback, and the Naming of Cybernetics
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Boarding House and the Father's Library

stops.name: Columbia, Missouri, birth in a boarding house
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (Segal, NAS Biographical Memoir 1992, p.391; MacTutor). The boarding house's address is not given in any source consulted, so the pin is city-centre Columbia and approximate. The Maimonides descent is family tradition recorded by Wiener himself, [R], with no genealogical demonstration anywhere reachable. Leo Wiener's Missouri appointment rests on Segal and MacTutor only: the English Wikipedia article on Leo Wiener does not mention it, and that disagreement is not resolved here
stops.campa: A son is born in a Columbia boarding house to Leo Wiener, philologist, and Bertha Kahn, daughter of a Missouri department-store owner, married the year before. The father takes the name Norbert out of a poem by Robert Browning. Leo was born in Bialystok, went from Warsaw to Berlin, abandoned a plan to found a Tolstoyan colony in Belize, and landed at New Orleans in steerage at eighteen with nothing in his pockets. The family holds, without any proof it can produce, that its line runs back to Moses Maimonides. Within a year the Missouri post is gone and the household is moving east.
suggested_refs: Leo Wiener's Harvard chair in Slavic languages, held 1896 to 1930
The family tradition of descent from Moses Maimonides, recorded in Wiener's own autobiographical volumes
sources: Irving Ezra Segal, 'Norbert Wiener 1894-1964,' National Academy of Sciences Biographical Memoir (1992), pp. 390-391
Wikipedia, 'Leon Lichtenstein' (Lichtenstein was cousin to Leo Wiener, not to Norbert's grandmother)

stops.name: Cambridge, the father's curriculum
stops.date_confidence: the move east is attested for 1895 (Segal p.391), but Leo Wiener's Harvard teaching begins in 1896 per Wikipedia, so the stop is dated to the Harvard footing rather than the departure; month and day are conventional. The childhood home's address was not established in any source consulted and the pin is approximate mid-Cambridge
stops.campa: Leo Wiener takes up Slavic languages at Harvard and keeps the post thirty-four years. At home he builds a curriculum for his son out of a large and unsystematic library: languages, mathematics, botany, chemistry, whatever the shelves hold. He drills the boy himself and corrects him without mercy, so that a wrong answer becomes a moral event. A son born in 1900 dies in infancy and another death follows in 1911. Three children survive after Norbert: Constance, Bertha, and Frederick. The boy is entered in a Cambridge public school in 1901, jumped from third grade to fourth, and pulled out again.
suggested_refs: The Peabody School, Cambridge, entered and left inside a year
Leo Wiener's home library, the entire syllabus of Norbert's childhood

stops.name: Ayer, high school among older boys
stops.date_confidence: the 1906 graduation is attested (Segal p.392); the 1903 entry year and the September month are inferred from a three-year course and are not documented
stops.campa: He is sent out to Ayer, west of Cambridge, to sit in a high school among students years older, a small boy in thick glasses who has already read past most of the syllabus. He graduates in 1906, eleven years old. The newspapers find him and print him as the most remarkable boy in the world. Leo gives interviews about the method that produced the result, and is glad to be asked. The son will not put his own account of any of it on paper until Ex-Prodigy, forty-seven years later.
suggested_refs: The 1906 newspaper coverage of the eleven-year-old Ayer graduate
Wiener's own retrospective volumes, Ex-Prodigy (1953) and I Am a Mathematician (1956)

stops.name: Ballou Hall, Medford, the degree at fourteen
stops.date_confidence: the cum laude A.B. in mathematics in 1909 at fourteen is attested (Segal p.392; Wikipedia; MacTutor); the June commencement month is conventional
stops.campa: Tufts takes him at eleven and turns him out at fourteen with an A.B. in mathematics, cum laude. He studies biology alongside it, because the microscope still interests him more than the proof does. Phi Beta Kappa passes him over. He is now a college graduate and, by his own later account, socially still a child, unable to hold the ordinary conversation of boys he has just outrun by four years. He goes home to Cambridge for the summer and enrolls at Harvard in the autumn.
suggested_refs: Ballou Hall, Tufts College, Medford, where the fourteen-year-old took his degree

segments.name: Zoology, Philosophy, and a Doctorate at Eighteen

stops.name: Harvard, the zoology laboratory
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1909-10 academic year (Segal pp.392-393; MacTutor); month conventional. The pin is the corpus's Harvard Yard pin; the specific laboratory building is not named in any source consulted
stops.campa: He enters the Harvard Graduate School meaning to become a zoologist. The laboratory defeats him inside a year. He cannot make his hands do what the work requires: the slide slips, the dissection tears, the thick glasses fog over the specimen at the eyepiece. Leo had chosen zoology for him, on the strength of an interest in the microscope the boy really did have. Leo now chooses again, and by the autumn of 1910 his son is a graduate student in philosophy, at fifteen, with the microscope packed away and no say in either decision.
suggested_refs: The Harvard zoological laboratories, abandoned within a year for want of manual dexterity

stops.name: Sage School, Ithaca, the black year
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1910-11 (Segal pp.392-393); the phrase 'black year' for 1911 is MacTutor's, drawn from Wiener's own account; month conventional. The pin is the corpus's Cornell pin, not a Sage Hall survey point
stops.campa: A scholarship carries him to Cornell's Sage School of Philosophy, where he reads under Frank Thilly, Walter Hammond, and Ernest Albee. He is fifteen and living away from the house for the first time, and he fails at it. He calls 1911 his black year afterwards: overextended, unhappy, quarrelling with himself about what he is and what he is for, a Jewish household's prodigy in a gentile faculty with no idea what to do with him. He goes back to Cambridge at the end of it.
suggested_refs: The Sage School of Philosophy, Cornell University, and the scholarship year of 1910-11

stops.name: Emerson Hall, the master's degree and the algebra of relatives
stops.date_confidence: the 1912 M.A. is tagged [R] in the research pool, resting on Segal p.393 alone; the 1913 Ph.D. under Karl Schmidt, after Royce's health failed, is attested (Segal p.393; MacTutor). The stop is dated to the doctorate; the month is conventional
stops.campa: Back at Harvard he works under Edward Huntington, George Herbert Palmer, Josiah Royce, and George Santayana, and takes the M.A. in 1912. Royce is to direct the doctorate, but Royce's health gives out and Karl Schmidt of Tufts takes the thesis instead. He submits a comparison of the algebra of relatives in Schroder against the version in Whitehead and Russell, and Harvard gives him the doctorate in philosophy in 1913. He is eighteen. Nobody in the department yet calls him a mathematician.
suggested_refs: Wiener's 1913 Harvard dissertation on the algebra of relatives in Schroder, Whitehead, and Russell

stops.name: Trinity College, Cambridge, Russell hands him to Hardy
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1913-14 fellowship year (Segal pp.393-394; MacTutor); the October month is conventional for the Michaelmas term. The pin is the corpus's canonical Trinity College pin
stops.campa: A Harvard traveling fellowship puts him in Cambridge to study mathematical logic with Bertrand Russell, whose Principia his thesis had been about. Russell reads him, tells him without softening it that a logician ignorant of mathematics is no use to anybody, and sends him to lectures. It is G. H. Hardy's course that takes: the Lebesgue integral, and rigour, and what an argument must do before it is allowed to stand. Wiener is still naming Hardy as his teacher thirty-four years later, in the obituary he writes when Hardy dies.
suggested_refs: G. H. Hardy's Cambridge lectures on the Lebesgue integral, 1913-14

stops.name: Cambridge, the ordered pair
stops.date_confidence: [A] for the 1914 paper 'A Simplification of the Logic of Relations' and for its content (Wikipedia, 'Ordered pair,' citing van Heijenoort 1967); van Heijenoort itself was not consulted. The pool originally dated this to the 1913 dissertation, which is wrong in both year and document. The exact reading date of 23 February 1914 is the figure in wide circulation and was NOT independently confirmed in this pass
stops.campa: He reads a short paper to the Cambridge Philosophical Society called A Simplification of the Logic of Relations. In it he does something Whitehead and Russell had not: he builds the ordered pair out of sets alone, so that the theory of relations needs no primitive notion of order at all. His construction is awkward, three nestings of braces deep. Kuratowski publishes a cleaner one in 1921 and it is Kuratowski's that survives into the textbooks. The move itself, that order can be manufactured out of unordered membership, is his, at nineteen.
suggested_refs: Wiener, 'A Simplification of the Logic of Relations' (1914), reprinted in van Heijenoort, From Frege to Godel (1967)
Kuratowski's 1921 definition of the ordered pair, which superseded it

stops.name: Gottingen, Hilbert and Landau and Husserl
stops.date_confidence: attested for the second semester of the fellowship year, cut short by the outbreak of war (Segal p.395; MacTutor); the April month is inferred from the summer semester and is not documented. The coordinate is the corpus's canonical Gottingen pin, inherited byte-identical from john_von_neumann.journey.json; it disagrees with the geography lens's 51.5347 / 9.9357 and with the corpus's more common 51.534 / 9.935, and the disagreement is recorded and not resolved
stops.campa: With Russell away for the second semester he crosses to Gottingen and sits in the rooms where the century's mathematics is being made: David Hilbert on differential equations, Edmund Landau on group theory, and Edmund Husserl in the philosophy faculty, still working out what a phenomenon is. He is nineteen and has now been taught by four of the men whose names the subject will keep. In August the war closes the town to him and he takes ship home. He will come back on a fellowship twelve years later.
suggested_refs: Hilbert's Gottingen lectures on differential equations, summer semester 1914
Husserl's Gottingen philosophy lectures of the same term

stops.name: Columbia University, the year with Dewey
stops.date_confidence: attested that the second fellowship year was spent at Columbia with John Dewey (Segal p.395); month conventional. The Bowdoin Prize in the same year comes from the uncorroborated crawl and is [R]. The pin is the corpus's canonical Columbia University pin
stops.campa: The second year of the fellowship is spent in New York, at Columbia, reading with John Dewey. Dewey's pragmatism, that an idea is a plan of action and is tested by what it does, sits oddly beside Hardy's rigour and beside Russell's logicism, and Wiener takes it anyway and keeps all three. He carries off Harvard's Bowdoin Prize the same year. The habit of standing in two disciplines at once, and being wholly trusted by neither, is set here. Then the fellowship money runs out. There is a year back at Harvard, 1915 into 1916, and after that nothing arranged.
suggested_refs: John Dewey's Columbia seminars, 1914-15

stops.name: Orono, the mathematics instructorship
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1916-17 (Segal p.395); month conventional. That the appointment ended badly is Wiener's own account as relayed by Segal and MacTutor, not an institutional record
stops.campa: He teaches mathematics for a year at the University of Maine, his first paid position, and it goes badly. The students are older than he is and they know it. He has lectured on the logic of geometry at Harvard, drilled with the Harvard reserve regiment at the Plattsburg training camp, and now stands in front of a class in Orono that will not hold still for him. The contract is not renewed, and he goes back to Massachusetts at twenty-two to look for anything at all. What actually happened in that classroom survives only in his own retelling of it, decades afterwards. Maine's side of the matter was never written down.
suggested_refs: The Officers' Training Camp at Plattsburg, New York, where he drilled in 1916

stops.name: Lynn, the turbine shop
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1917 (Segal p.395); month conventional. The Albany Encyclopedia Americana post, 1917-18, is attested in the same passage but has no stop of its own in this file
stops.campa: General Electric takes him on as an apprentice engineer in the turbine department at Lynn. He is put among machines and among men who work with their hands, which is the one thing his hands have never been able to do. He lasts months. From Lynn he goes to Albany to write entries for the Encyclopedia Americana, a paid position for a man who has read everything and can be trusted with a fact. He is at that desk through 1917 and into 1918, writing to assigned length on subjects assigned to him by other men.
suggested_refs: The General Electric turbine works at Lynn, Massachusetts
The Encyclopedia Americana editorial offices at Albany, New York, 1917-18

stops.name: Aberdeen Proving Ground, the ballistic tables
stops.date_confidence: the January 1918 letter to his father is attested and quoted verbatim in Segal pp.395-396; the Aberdeen service, civilian then enlisted, and the February 1919 discharge are attested in the same passage and in MacTutor. The coordinate is inherited byte-identical from john_von_neumann.journey.json, which carries an Aberdeen stop of its own for 1940
stops.campa: In January he writes to his father asking permission to seek military service. He goes to Maryland, to Oswald Veblen's computing unit at Aberdeen Proving Ground, and joins the men grinding out ballistic tables: firing angle against range, corrected for wind and air density, column after column of numbers that end at the muzzle of a gun. He works first as a civilian and then enlists as a private in the United States Army, and is discharged in February 1919. Veblen does not take him on to Princeton.
stops.quote: I think the time has come for me to make a last try to get into military service, and I am writing to ask you for permission. . . . It is not that I am dissatisfied with my work nor that I have any particular love for a military career, but I hate to think of myself as less of a man than those of my friends who are in the army, and I do not care after this war to look back on myself as a slacker. I cannot be anything but ashamed of myself when I advocate a war that I do not share in.
stops.quote_source: Norbert Wiener to his father Leo Wiener, January 1918, quoted verbatim in Irving Ezra Segal, 'Norbert Wiener 1894-1964,' National Academy of Sciences Biographical Memoir (1992), p.395
suggested_refs: Oswald Veblen's ballistic-table computing unit at Aberdeen Proving Ground, 1918

stops.name: Boston, out of the Herald
stops.date_confidence: [R]. That he worked briefly for the Boston Herald in 1919 and was dismissed is in the crawl; the REASON is contradicted between sources and is not resolved here. Wikipedia's wikitext says he was fired for reluctance to write favourable articles about a politician the owners wanted promoted; the crawl's other version has him refusing to write up conditions in the Lawrence mills. No reachable document adjudicates. Month and day are conventional
stops.campa: He takes editorial work at the Boston Herald and is out of it within months. He was asked to write something he did not believe and declined to write it; on whose behalf, a politician the owners wanted promoted or the mill owners of Lawrence, the record disagrees with itself and will not say. Five positions in three years, every one of them ended, and he is twenty-four with a Harvard doctorate and an army discharge and nothing to do on Monday. Which version of the dismissal is the true one has never been settled. Both accounts are still in circulation, and nothing reachable adjudicates between them.
suggested_refs: The Boston Herald newsroom, 1919, and the dismissal whose cause the sources dispute
sources: Uncorroborated dossier crawl (Lawrence mills version), flagged and not adopted

stops.name: MIT, hired on Osgood's word
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1919 (Segal p.396; MacTutor; MIT News, 'Timeline: Norbert Wiener'); month conventional. The 1932 professorship and 1959 Institute Professorship are attested in MacTutor. The pin is the corpus's canonical MIT pin, inherited from claude_shannon.journey.json
stops.campa: W. F. Osgood of the Harvard mathematics department recommends him across the river, and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology hires him as an instructor. MIT in 1919 is an engineering school with no standing whatever in pure mathematics, which is exactly why it will suit him: nobody here will tell him that a problem in physics is beneath a mathematician. He is twenty-four when he arrives and he never leaves. Instructor in 1919, professor in 1932, Institute Professor in 1959, all of it at the one address, and he is still on the faculty in the year he dies.
suggested_refs: W. F. Osgood's 1919 recommendation, the hinge of the whole career

stops.name: Paris, the letter to Constance
stops.date_confidence: attested to August 1920, quoted verbatim in Segal p.397; the day is not recorded. The pin is the corpus's canonical Paris pin
stops.campa: In Paris in August he writes to his sister Constance that he is trying to reach Maurice Frechet and is making headway on a problem he calls integration in function space. The question is whether one can put a measure on a space whose points are entire curves, so that a set of paths has a size the way a set of numbers has a length. Russell had told him years earlier to look at Brownian motion. He is now doing both at once, in a rented room, waiting on a telegram from a man he has not met.
stops.quote: I have not been able so far to get in touch with Frechet. I have wired him that I am here and awaiting an answer. I find that I am making a little headway with my problem, integration in function space, and in a way that may have practical application. I define the measure of an interval in it in a way that hitches up with probability theory as it is applied in statistical mechanics, and I have been living in hopes that the Lebesgue integral which I can get from it will be good for something. At any rate, when I meet Frechet, I shall have a peach of a problem to work on.
stops.quote_source: Norbert Wiener to his sister Constance, Paris, August 1920, quoted in Irving Ezra Segal, NAS Biographical Memoir (1992), p.397. The original punctuates 'my problem, integration in function space,' with dashes; they are rendered as commas here
suggested_refs: Maurice Frechet's Paris seminar on abstract spaces, the destination of the 1920 trip

stops.name: Strasbourg, the congress
stops.date_confidence: attested that he attended the 1920 Strasbourg International Congress of Mathematicians (MacTutor); the 22 September opening date is the congress's own and is background, not a pool claim. The exclusion of mathematicians of the defeated powers from that congress is likewise background from the congress's history and is not sourced from the research pool
stops.campa: He goes on to Strasbourg for the International Congress of Mathematicians, the first held since the war and the first from which the organizers bar the mathematicians of the defeated powers. The men he had gone to Gottingen to hear six years earlier are not admitted to it; their country lost the war. He is twenty-five, an instructor from an engineering school with no reputation in mathematics, carrying a half-finished idea about how to measure a set of curves. He presents it. Then he takes the boat home to Cambridge.
suggested_refs: The 1920 International Congress of Mathematicians at Strasbourg, held under the exclusion of the Central Powers

stops.name: MIT, the measure on path space
stops.date_confidence: the construction of Wiener measure is attested to the early 1920s (Segal pp.397-398; MacTutor); no single date exists for it and 1921 is chosen to order the segment, with the month conventional. The function-space problem came from I. A. Barnett and the Brownian motion from Russell's suggestion, both per MacTutor
stops.campa: He finishes it. The Brownian motion of a particle in a fluid was already physics: Einstein and Smoluchowski had written the fundamental papers on where a particle is at a given time. What nobody had asked was what kind of curve a single particle traces, and the answer, which Jean Perrin had guessed in Les Atomes, is one of those continuous nowhere-differentiable monsters the mathematicians had built as pathologies to be shunned. Wiener puts a measure on the space of those paths. The pathology turns out to be the generic case.
stops.quote: The Brownian motion was nothing new as an object of study by physicists. There were fundamental papers by Einstein and Smoluchowski that covered it, but whereas these papers concerned what was happening to any given particle at a specific time, or the long-time statistics of many particles, they did not concern themselves with the mathematical properties of the curve followed by a single particle. Here the literature was very scant, but it did include a telling comment by the French physicist Perrin in his book Les Atomes, where he said in effect that the very irregular curves followed by particles in the Brownian motion led one to think of the supposed continuous non-differentiable curves of the mathematicians.
stops.quote_source: Wiener's own retrospective account of the Brownian-motion work, quoted in Irving Ezra Segal, NAS Biographical Memoir (1992), p.411
suggested_refs: Jean Perrin, Les Atomes (1913), whose remark on the irregular curve Wiener took as a programme
The Wiener criterion for regularity of a boundary point, from the potential theory of the same years

stops.name: Cambridge, Massachusetts, the marriage to Margaret Engemann
stops.date_confidence: the 1926 marriage is attested (Segal p.399), the month and day are not recorded and the stop is dated to the head of the year so it precedes the April Guggenheim tenure. The daughters' 1928 and 1929 births are tagged [R] in the research pool and the birthplace is inferred, not documented
stops.campa: He marries Margaret Engemann, who came from Germany with her family as a girl and took degrees at Utah State College and at Radcliffe. She runs the house and, increasingly, the man: his sleep, his moods, his correspondence, the arrangements for the long tours he could never organize himself. Until this year his whole life had happened within walking distance of a desk. Their daughter Barbara is born in 1928, and a second daughter, Margaret, in 1929.
suggested_refs: Margaret Engemann Wiener, who accompanied him on every late lecture tour including the last

stops.name: Gottingen, the Guggenheim year
stops.date_confidence: the fellowship is attested precisely by the Guggenheim Foundation's own fellow record: awarded 1926 in Mathematics, ten months' tenure beginning 1 April 1926, with the citation quoted in the campa. CONTRADICTION NOT RESOLVED: Segal p.399 has the year split between Gottingen, arranged through Max Born, and Copenhagen with Harald Bohr; MacTutor's account of the same year runs Cambridge with Hardy then Gottingen and never mentions Copenhagen. No Copenhagen stop is written and that omission may be an omission of a real leg. Same canonical-pin disagreement as the 1914 Gottingen stop
stops.campa: A Guggenheim Fellowship, ten months from the first of April, is awarded for researches on Bohr's almost periodic functions, on haphazard motion, on periodogram analysis, and other topics. He spends part of it in Cambridge with Hardy and part of it back at Gottingen, in Richard Courant's circle, having arranged the visit through Max Born. Twelve years earlier he had come here at nineteen to watch Hilbert lecture, and had gone home in August when the war shut the town. He is thirty-one now and the Brownian motion carries his name. Whether the ten months also took him to Copenhagen, to Harald Bohr, the accounts disagree.
suggested_refs: The Guggenheim Foundation fellow record for 1926, giving the citation and the ten-month tenure from 1 April
Harald Bohr's theory of almost periodic functions, the fellowship's stated subject
sources: John Simon Guggenheim Foundation, fellow record, 'Norbert Wiener'

segments.name: Harmonic Analysis and the English Year

stops.name: MIT, from harmonic analysis to the Tauberian theorems
stops.date_confidence: Generalized Harmonic Analysis 1930 and the hundred-page Tauberian Theorems 1932 are attested (Segal pp.399-400); the share of the Bocher Memorial Prize in 1933 is attested in Wikipedia. Month and day conventional; the stop gathers three dated events at one address
stops.campa: Generalized Harmonic Analysis appears in 1930, a long memoir turning the machinery he built for Brownian paths onto functions along a line: what frequencies does a signal contain when it never repeats and never dies away? Two years later he publishes a hundred pages of Tauberian theorems, welding Hardy and Littlewood's methods to Robert Schmidt's group-theoretic ones, and takes a share of the Bocher Prize for it in 1933. In the same decade he had solved the Dirichlet problem in general and given a geometric test for a regular boundary point, still called the Wiener criterion.
suggested_refs: Wiener, 'Generalized Harmonic Analysis,' Acta Mathematica (1930)
Wiener, 'Tauberian Theorems,' Annals of Mathematics (1932), and the 1933 Bocher Memorial Prize

stops.name: Cambridge, the year with Hardy
stops.date_confidence: the Cambridge year producing The Fourier Integral and Certain of Its Applications (1933) is attested in MacTutor; the October start is conventional. The Wiener-Hopf collaboration is attested to the early 1930s (Segal pp.400-401) and took place at MIT, not in Cambridge; it is named here because MacTutor pairs the two, and the geography is stated plainly in the campa
stops.campa: He spends an academic year in Cambridge working near Hardy, and the lectures become The Fourier Integral and Certain of Its Applications, published by the University Press in 1933. In the same stretch he brings Eberhard Hopf out to MIT, and the two of them produce the integral equation that carries both their names, a method for problems whose kernel depends only on the difference of its arguments. Physicists will still be solving it for diffraction and radiative transfer decades afterwards, and Wiener himself will use it to predict a signal from its own past.
stops.quote: I think it is fair to say that throughout their long collaboration the extremes of technical facility belong to Littlewood, but that much of the nexus of leading ideas and the philosophical unity is that of Hardy.
stops.quote_source: Wiener, from his obituary of G. H. Hardy, quoted in Irving Ezra Segal, NAS Biographical Memoir (1992), p.401
suggested_refs: Wiener, The Fourier Integral and Certain of Its Applications (Cambridge University Press, 1933)
The Wiener-Hopf equation and its later use in diffraction and prediction

stops.name: Vienna, the rooms still full
stops.date_confidence: attested only as 'early-to-mid 1930s' European travel (MacTutor), naming Blaschke, Karl Menger, Artin, Godel, and Hahn; 1933 is chosen to order the segment and the month is conventional. The Berlin leg of the same circuit is not separately pinned. NOTE for the corpus: the Vienna figure is Karl Menger the mathematician (1902-1985), NOT Carl Menger the economist (1840-1921), who is a separate atlas subject
stops.campa: On the continental circuits of these years he calls on Wilhelm Blaschke and on Karl Menger, and in Menger's Vienna colloquium he meets Emil Artin, Hans Hahn, and Kurt Godel. Godel is in his twenties and has already published the theorem that ends Hilbert's programme, the same programme Wiener had watched Hilbert expound at Gottingen in 1914. The rooms he moves through in Europe are still full of people. Within a few years many of them will be writing to him from Cambridge, asking for help getting out.
suggested_refs: Karl Menger's Vienna mathematical colloquium of the early 1930s
The Emergency Committee in Aid of Displaced German Scholars, through which Wiener later placed refugees

stops.name: MIT, Paley and the strings drawn tight
stops.date_confidence: the 1932-33 collaboration, Paley's accidental death, and the 1934 publication of Fourier Transforms in the Complex Domain are attested (Segal pp.400-401), with Wiener's account of the division of labour quoted verbatim. The MANNER of Paley's death is not specified in any source reached in this pass and is deliberately not stated. Month and day conventional
stops.campa: R. E. A. C. Paley comes over from England, young and formidably quick, and for something over a year the two of them work as a single machine. Then Paley is killed in an accident. What kind of accident is not stated in anything that has survived to be read. Wiener finishes what they had between them and publishes it in 1934 as Fourier Transforms in the Complex Domain, under both names, with an account of the division of labour that hands the younger man the harder half of it.
stops.quote: My role was primarily that of suggesting problems and the broad lines on which they might be attacked, and it was generally left to Paley to draw the strings tight.
stops.quote_source: Wiener on his collaboration with R. E. A. C. Paley, quoted in Irving Ezra Segal, NAS Biographical Memoir (1992), p.400
suggested_refs: Paley and Wiener, Fourier Transforms in the Complex Domain (American Mathematical Society, 1934), completed after Paley's death

segments.name: Peiping, the Predictor, and the Naming

stops.name: Tsing Hua, Peiping, the visiting professorship
stops.date_confidence: [R]: the 1935-36 Tsing Hua visiting professorship rests on Segal p.404 alone and is so tagged in the research pool; month conventional. The coordinate is the old Tsing Hua campus and is approximate. The refugee-placement work through the China Aid Society and the Emergency Committee comes from the uncorroborated crawl citing Segal and was not independently refetched
stops.campa: He goes to China for the academic year as visiting professor at Tsing Hua University in Peiping, and learns to speak the language with a fluency his colleagues remark on. He publishes there in the analytic tradition he had taken from Hardy and Littlewood. He also acquires a student and a lifelong friend in Yuk-Wing Lee, and a set of obligations: as the decade closes he works through the China Aid Society and the Emergency Committee in Aid of Displaced German Scholars to place Lee, Antoni Zygmund, and others in American positions.
suggested_refs: Tsing Hua University, Peiping, old campus, 1935-36
Yuk-Wing Lee, Wiener's Chinese student and later MIT colleague
sources: Uncorroborated dossier crawl citing Segal for the refugee work

stops.name: MIT, the antiaircraft predictor
stops.date_confidence: the NDRC predictor work with Julian Bigelow is attested for the war years (Segal pp.405-406); the geography lens dates the project 1940-1943 and the month is conventional. CORRECTED from the pool: the wartime report was published as a book in 1949, not 1950 (OpenLibrary: first_publish_year 1949, Technology Press of MIT / Wiley; the 1964 MIT Press reissue explains the later dates in circulation). The black-box framing and the Benzedrine testimony come from the crawl citing Peter Galison and Wiener's own words, not independently refetched
stops.campa: Under Vannevar Bush's National Defense Research Committee he takes up the antiaircraft gun. A shell needs ten to twenty seconds to reach a bomber, so the gunner must fire at where the plane will be. With the engineer Julian Bigelow he models pilot and aircraft together as one box with an input and an output, and asks only what the box does, never what is inside it. The device never reaches the prediction horizon combat requires. The mathematics does: noise as a stationary Gaussian process, and a filter that pulls the signal out of it. He computes through the nights on Benzedrine, to the serious detriment, he writes afterwards, of his health.
suggested_refs: Wiener, Extrapolation, Interpolation, and Smoothing of Stationary Time Series (Technology Press of MIT and Wiley, 1949), the declassified wartime report
Andrey Kolmogorov's parallel Soviet prediction theory of the same years, unknown to Wiener until after the war
sources: Uncorroborated dossier crawl citing Peter Galison

stops.name: Mexico City, Avenida Cuauhtemoc, the tremor and the gun
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Rosenblueth collaboration ran from 1945 onward in repeated visits (crawl citing Segal, not independently refetched); month and day conventional. stops.campa: He goes down to the Instituto Nacional de Cardiologia on Avenida Cuauhtemoc, in the Colonia Doctores, and works with Arturo Rosenblueth, who had been Walter Cannon's man at Harvard and is now Mexico's. They study cardiac conduction and muscular clonus: a limb that overshoots its target, swings back, overshoots again, which is precisely what the antiaircraft predictor did when its feedback was set too high. The gun and the tremor are one failure wearing two coats. He returns to Mexico for the rest of his life.

Warren McCulloch chairs. stops.campa: A researcher at Boeing writes asking for a copy of his wartime work bearing on a guided-missile project. He is fifty-two, and he refuses, and then he publishes the refusal. stops.campa: The book comes out of a seminar he has run since the war, where Bigelow, Y. W. Lee, Rosenblueth, McCulloch, Walter Rosenblith, Jerome Wiesner, and Walter Pitts sit in one room and refuse to stay inside their departments. He names the field cybernetics, from the Greek for steersman, and defines it as control and communication in the animal and the machine, one subject and not two. MIT and Wiley publish in October; Hermann et Cie of Paris publish the French edition simultaneously. Claude Shannon's information theory, out of Bell Laboratories that same year, is the sharpest concrete instance of the claim.

stops.name: Cambridge, the letter to Walter Reuther
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the letter's published text is at libcom.org. CORRECTED from the pool, which excerpted 'the unemployment produced by such plants can only be disastrous' while dropping the conditional clause that opens the sentence; the full sentence is quoted here, because Wiener conditions the disaster on the ownership arrangement and not on automation as such
stops.campa: On the thirteenth of August he writes to Walter Reuther, president of the United Automobile Workers, to tell him what is coming. The apparatus he helped build will lead, he says, to the factory without employees, the automatic automobile assembly line, and a critical situation is bound to arise under any condition in some ten to twenty years. Three years earlier he refused to sell the technique to a bomber manufacturer. Now he offers it, free and unasked, to a union, on the argument that the men who will be replaced should hear about it before the men doing the replacing.
stops.quote: In the hands of the present industrial set-up, the unemployment produced by such plants can only be disastrous.
stops.quote_source: Wiener to Walter Reuther, president of the United Automobile Workers, 13 August 1949; published text at libcom.org

stops.name: Cambridge, the second edition of The Human Use of Human Beings
stops.date_confidence: the revised second edition is Doubleday Anchor, 1954; month and day conventional. CORRECTED from the pool, which cited the quoted passage to the 1950 first edition: the full OCR of the 1950 Houghton Mifflin text was downloaded and grepped and contains no occurrence of 'whirlpool,' 'abides,' 'perpetuate themselves,' or 'ever-flowing,' and has no chapter titled 'Organization as the Message' at all. The wording is also corrected: 'not stuff that abides,' without the article. Page cite via Terrell Ward Bynum, arXiv:1802.02029v2, citing Wiener 1954, 96; the 1954 text itself was not located online and the page number is therefore second-hand
stops.campa: He rewrites the popular book of 1950 for Doubleday Anchor, and the revision is not a tidying. Whole chapters are new, among them one called Organization as the Message, in which he asks what a person is once you have decided that the thing which persists is a pattern and not a substance. The body replaces its own material continuously. What continues is the arrangement. He is fifty-nine, and the argument he is making about human beings is the argument he made about a Brownian path in 1921: the object of study is the shape, not the stuff.
stops.quote: We are but whirlpools in a river of ever-flowing water. We are not stuff that abides, but patterns that perpetuate themselves.
stops.quote_source: Wiener, The Human Use of Human Beings, second edition revised (Doubleday Anchor, 1954), ch. V, 'Organization as the Message,' p.96
suggested_refs: The Human Use of Human Beings, 2nd ed. revised (Doubleday Anchor, 1954; Da Capo reprint 1988), whose chapter II carries the line that progress imposes not only new possibilities for the future but new restrictions

stops.name: UCLA, the summer of prediction
stops.date_confidence: attested that he taught repeated summers at UCLA across 1953-1963, including prediction lectures in 1953 (crawl citing Segal, not independently refetched); month conventional. stops.campa: He teaches summer courses in Los Angeles, at UCLA, and returns across the following decade. The 1953 lectures are on prediction: given a signal buried in noise and a record of its past, what is the best guess at its next value, and how much better can no method whatever do? It is the antiaircraft problem with the aircraft taken out. Andrey Kolmogorov had reached the same results in Moscow during the war, and Wiener did not know it until an American colleague happened to mention it to him at a meeting.

stops.name: Yale, the Terry Lectures
stops.date_confidence: the 1962 Terry Lectures under the title 'Prolegomena to Theology' are attested (crawl citing Segal, not independently refetched); month and day conventional. That the golem is Wiener's working figure is taken from the eventual book's title and subject, God & Golem, Inc., attested at Segal p.408
stops.campa: He gives the Terry Lectures at Yale under the title Prolegomena to Theology. The subject is what cybernetics does to three old religious questions: whether a machine can learn, whether a machine can make another machine in its own image, and what a man owes for the thing he has made. His working figure is the golem of Prague, the creature animated by a written word and obedient well past the point where obedience is safe. He has been making the same argument about who answers for a machine since the Boeing letter of 1946. He is sixty-seven.
suggested_refs: The 1962 Dwight Harrington Terry Lectures at Yale, 'Prolegomena to Theology'

stops.campa: At the abbey of Royaumont north of Paris he gives the presentation that joins with the Yale material into a single short book. He publishes it as God & Golem, Inc.: A Comment on Certain Points Where Cybernetics Impinges on Religion. The argument is that the sorcerer's apprentice is not a fable about magic but a description of engineering practice, because a machine given a goal will pursue the goal as stated and not the goal as meant, and the gap between those two is where the disaster lives.
